utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. I hope you have had a good time during Easter, and we start again with this case. First of all, we are sitting only with two Judges today because Judge Mindua is not present due to another commitment, and we are sitting pursuant Rule 15 bis. The next witness, I think, is available and could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. You are here as a witness. You are welcome to the Tribunal, and you must know there are some protective measures in place like the last time. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Thayer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer is starting the examination-in-chief, and please, both parties should be reminded that you should always switch off the microphone when the witness is answering because of the protective measures. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, and good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we get underway, I would just ask with the assistance of Madam Usher if you look at the sheet that's being shown to you, and without stating any information that's on the sheet, can you confirm that you see your name on that document, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd ask that that be handed up to the Chamber. Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender the pseudonym sheet, 65 ter number 6207, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P95 under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask you a couple of questions to affirm your testimony from the prior trial. Do you recall testifying, in fact in this very courtroom, a little over three years ago in another trial?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And have you recently had an opportunity to listen to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, if you were asked the same questions today as you were asked in that other trial would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time the Prosecution would offer 65 ter 6202, which is under seal, the witness's testimony in the prior case, as well as 65 ter 6203, the public redacted version of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Both will be received, the first under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 6202 will be Exhibit P96 under seal. 6203 will be Exhibit P97, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may go into private session for the only question I have for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We had a longer period of private session as expected because of some technical problems here in the courtroom. Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The witness was born and raised in the Zvornik municipality. In May 1992, Serb shelling forced him to the Cerska area. The witness was able to return to his village, but in January 1993, a Serb offensive forced him to flee again to the Cerska area from where the offensive pushed him to Konjevic Polje, and then to Srebrenica. With respect to events in Srebrenica in 1993, the witness described the humanitarian conditions in March and events concerning General Morillon, the departure of civilians on empty UNHCR trucks, and the shelling of a playground that killed approximately 60 people at around the time Srebrenica was declared a safe area. The witness also described the humanitarian conditions prevailing in Srebrenica in 1995, the decrease in aid convoys, and the wounding of civilians by sniping and shelling prior to the fall of the enclave. With respect to the Serb attack on Srebrenica in July 1995, the witness testified about soldiers and civilians being wounded and killed, shelling that damaged the hospital, the movement of civilians towards Potocari, and the column of Muslim men, which he joined on 11 July. The witness testified that his small group became separated from the column and spent several days moving in the woods until they reached the area of Snagovo. As they prepared tea for a sick member of the group, Serb soldiers appeared, surrounded them, and ordered them to put their hands up. The witness and his group were bound behind their backs, taken a short distance where they were thrown to the ground and beaten. The Serb soldiers had insignia stating something to the effect of, and I quote, "police of Republika Srpska." The witness did not have any identification documents, so when his captors questioned him about his particulars, he lied about his family and his age so that they would think that he was much younger than he was. One of the Serb soldiers was assigned to be with the witness at all times. The witness and this Serb soldier walked a short distance further, after which the witness heard a burst of gunfire and individual shots. The witness was panicked and shaking, so the soldier tried to console him and later gave him food and water. The witness never saw or heard from the other men in his group again after their capture. While with the Serb soldiers, the witness slept among them and was restrained, but not the entire time. He was then bused to a command building, interrogated and sent to the Batkovic camp where he stayed for several months. That concludes the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. No more examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I've concluded the examination-in-chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, now it is the right of the accused to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir, please start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. God help everybody in the courtroom and everybody who is following my case. It is my wish for this case to end, God willingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I will have a few questions for you. When I say "thank you," could you then start answering, this in order to avoid overlapping as a result of the fact that we both speak the same language. First of all, do you want to explain the reasons for protective measures? Why did you insist on testifying under protective measures both in the Popovic case and in this case?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: For my own security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You confirmed in your testimony in the Popovic case on pages 40 to 43, lines 18 and 19 that you moved into the country where you now reside as an illegal immigrant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When was it? What year? When did you leave Bosnia-Herzegovina and enter the third country illegally? I don't want to mention its name.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: It was some 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Some 15 years ago therefore. Thank you. Could you please describe the illegal residence in the country where you arrived? I insist on you telling me who assisted you in arriving there, and how did you manage to enter that country illegally?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: This is my own private matter. It was not easy to travel illegally, and I took care of my travel arrangements myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have the right to answer. I suppose the Trial Chamber will be interested in learning the details, and I leave it to them. When you -- when did you enter the third country where you now reside, and did you immediately request asylum?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I entered the country, I requested the asylum immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you apply for residence, and what reasons did you give for applying for residence?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. I don't think it's even important. And the reasons are stated was the things that happened during the war and the consequences that I suffer. Those were the main reasons why I left my place of birth and why I decided to live in a third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that when you apply for residence you have to state some reasons for that, and -- and when you travel, even illegally, you had to state reasons for travel. Maybe you travelled as a tourist, but even if that was the case, you had to state that as well. Did you provide any statements to the government of the country in which you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Those statements were very short because I travelled illegally, without any ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you because every country where an illegal immigrant arrives wants to know what they think and what they intend to do, and I'm sure that they want to hear the reasons.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Of course they wanted to have my statement. First of all, they wanted to know how I travelled, and second of all, the reasons for which I left my country after the war. They wanted to hear what had happened to me and to my family, and those are the reasons that I stated for wanting to remain in that third country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you very shortly. Please pause a little bit more after a question because of the translation. They can't catch your full answer if you start answering too fast. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, at the time when you arrived as an illegal alien, were you in contact with anybody from the Prosecutor's office, either openly or also illegally?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No, not at that time. Not during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When was it that you got in touch with the OTP for the first time, and when did you provide your first statement to them?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I would put it the other way round. It was them who got in touch with me. I can't give you the exact date because I don't remember, but I believe that it was in May 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 1D68. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be double sure, Mr. President, this needs to not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the registry will do everything what is needed for that. Mr. Tolimir, now we have it on the screen, and the witness can see the document. Now you can ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to look at this document during your proofing session?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this document, but this document does not bear my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did the OTP ask you to sign a statement, which is customary?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case, on page 3987, you confirmed that you had refused to testify before you were granted permanent residence. Is it true that -- did it have an impact on you providing your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Of course I insisted on permanent residence before I appeared before this Tribunal. I wanted to be granted permanent residence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The fact that the document does not bear your signature has something to do with the fact that you insisted on permanent residence in the third country in which you had resided at the time?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You applied for permanent resistance [as interpreted] in 2001, and you were only granted that permanent residence when Mr. McCloskey intervened.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I can't answer the question as to what was instrumental to me being granted permanent a resistance [as interpreted]. I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you not answer because you don't know or you are not allowed to tell?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: When I was given permanent residence, I read it but there were there were no -- there was no statement of reasons as to why I had been granted permanent residence, but it does say in that decision that

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: (redacted). They sent me a decision on permanent residence in which they stated that between the year 2003 and 2006 I was a resident, but I was never handed the decision on permanent residence. And in the decision it also stated what legal remedies I had at my disposal, that I had the right to appeal. I never appealed. I didn't launch an appeal. There were some games behind all that, and it happens a lot of times. It's not an uncommon situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to remind you again to pause between question and answer, and please slow down a little bit. Everything has to be interpreted, and the interpreters don't catch everything what you are telling us. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand we went into open session, and we're going to need a redaction at page 13 of our LiveNote, anyway, line 15. I know there are slightly different pages for the Chamber, but there's a reference there to a location. I would just ask that that be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are right. That will be redacted. Mr. Tolimir, please continue, but slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can we then conclude that it was only after you were provided documents in the country where you resided, it was only that -- then that your problem with the statement and its signing before the OTP was resolved?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: When I appeared before this Tribunal last time, I still had not been provided with any documents. However, after a short while I was provided with permanent residence documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you openly say to the OTP that you would not testify before you were granted permanent residence in a European country?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what did the OTP say to that? Can you just tell us briefly in one sentence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: (redacted) and they're the only ones who can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Please don't repeat again the name of the country. You again mentioned that. We have to redact that. Please bear that in mind. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us, while you were waiting for a decision on permanent residence in a European country, did the OTP contact you either formally or informally? Did they take statements from you without signature?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No. The first time they came in touch with me, as I've already told you, was in May 2006, not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you told us just a while ago that you said that you would only testify if you were granted a residence in a European country. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I repeat that my first contact with the OTP was in 2006. However, at that point in time it didn't -- I did not have a permanent residence in any European country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put it this way: Did the OTP help you in any way to become a resident in a European country?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I can't answer that question now because I don't know. I don't know whether they exerted any influence or not. It would be the ministry that provided me with the residence who would be able to tell you that. They would be the best suited to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you told them that you would not testify before you were given residence. Were you first provided residence and then came to testify or the other way round? What happened?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No. I did not have permanent residence when I came to testify. I decided to testify in the hope that in a short while I would be provided a permanent residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise. In the Popovic transcript, you said that you became resident on Mr. McCloskey's intervention; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you then provide a wrong statement? Did you misspeak?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I became resident when I finished that testimony in The Hague and when I returned home. A couple of days later I became resident. I was provided with permanent residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say you returned home. What do you mean, when you returned here? When you returned where?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: In the country where I resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In any case, can you please answer. When you said in the Popovic case that you would not testify before you were granted residence, did the Trial Chamber or the OTP help you get residence?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, they did try. They probably wrote a letter and sent it. Whether that had any influence on the decision to grant residence, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please just tell me this: Did you consider it your duty to testify regardless of the help that you expected in order to resolve this issue of residence? Is it every citizen's duty to testify?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No, it is not every citizen's duty. It is a personal decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't consider testifying before a court an obligation, either legal or moral?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No. It is my own personal decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you actually make it conditional on testifying to obtain this residence permit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, could you please repeat your question one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you make it a condition when you talked to the Prosecution that you would testify it on condition that you would get a permanent residence, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you describe what kind of conditions you set?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think -- I think both speakers should really slow down and pause between question and answer. The interpreters can't catch everything. There's always an overlap. You can see that sometimes on the screen. Mr. Thayer, you wanted to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I did, Mr. President. The witness answered the question, but I think we've had about 15 minutes, I think, worth of questioning on this same issue, and the witness's answers have remained the same no matter how many different ways the question has been asked. I think it's beginning to cross the line of utility for the Trial Chamber in fairness, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was also the concern of the Chamber. Mr. Tolimir, I think what you wanted to know you got from the witness. Please continue, perhaps with another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since Mr. Thayer does not want us to explore this any further, whereas it was part of his statement, I will now move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the summary of your statement the Prosecutor briefly mentions your statement regarding General Morillon's presence in Srebrenica in 1993, and it was stated here in public session that you've testified about that as well. On page 3293 of the Popovic transcript, in answer to the Prosecutor's question whether you were present in person when General Morillon arrived in March 1993, you said, "Yes, I was present." You said that he was by the post office building, and, "I was there in front of it with a mass of people who were seeking to obtain some help," but then when they asked you whether you were in any contact with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the -- could the accused please repeat the last portion of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we don't receive English translation at the moment. You were asked by the interpreters to repeat the last portion of your question. Perhaps you did it, but we didn't receive English translation. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked the witness whether he was present in person when General Morillon arrived in March 1993, and he said that he was. That's what he said in the Popovic case, and I quote: "I was present. He was by the post office, and I was next to it in a mass of people who were seeking assistance from Morillon." But in answer to the question whether you personally participated in any operation -- in any action that had to do anything with General Morillon while he was in Srebrenica, he briefly replied, "No." So this was my quotation of his earlier testimony, so that now I can move on to my question. Do you allow me to put that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, tell us, please, how did it come about that this group of people, mass of people, gathered in Srebrenica when General Morillon arrived there in March 1993, and were you told to gather there by anyone, and were you informed that General Morillon would be coming? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: In March 1993, when Morillon arrived, of course all the people were in Srebrenica. They were gathered there. Srebrenica is a small place. There is one main street. It is -- it was full of people from several surrounding municipalities, and at the time when it was -- when we were wondering whether it would fall or not, at that point in time General Morillon appeared, and the people there saw the only -- the only way they could save themselves in General Morillon, and of course they gather there expecting to hear what the outcome would be and what to do next, and this means that I, too, walking there, walking by, saw this huge group of people. I asked them, because I was interested what was going on, and then I learned that Morillon was there and that he was the one who would actually take the final decision on Srebrenica and its future. Women, children, and younger people actually surrounded the post office building, the facilities where he was, until he took a decision that would be satisfying for that people, which means that I was there in the immediate vicinity, and I, too, was awaiting to hear what the information would be, whether it would be good or bad for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see document 1D69 on the screens. This is an OTP document from the proofing notes of the 14th November 2006, preceding his testimony in the Popovic says. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see the document before you, Witness? Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please take a look at the third paragraph. Can you see it? In the third paragraph it reads, I quote: "He was present when General Morillon arrived, and he was among those who blocked the APC." Have you found that? Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: However, in the Popovic case, on transcript page 4000, you said, I quote: "I was in the immediate vicinity of the building where he was, although I did not get in any kind of contact with him." And then on page 4003, 17 through 19, you said, I quote: "I was with a group of people there, but the women and children had blocked Morillon so that he would remain there until some kind of resolution was found in terms of the declaration of Srebrenica as a safe zone." And when it says here in the proofing notes that you were in a group of people who blocked Morillon and his APCs, you said that that was incorrect. "I was in the immediate vicinity of the place where Morillon was." Is all of this what I've just mentioned here correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, yes. I've tried to explain in answer to your question that I was not a participant or an organiser of this event. I repeat, these were women and children. But I was in that large group of people awaiting the final solution and response. So there was no action. I didn't take any action. I just stayed there as a passer-by.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. I don't have any problem with that, but I would like you to explain both to me and to the Trial Chamber where this difference in your statement actually is coming from. First you said that you were in the group of people that had blocked General Morillon, and now you're saying that you weren't in the group, that you just happened to be there. So tell us which is true? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, in addition to the group there was this large long column, if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we need to make clear that we're not talking about a statement of this witness. As the general knows, what he is referring to is a proofing note of which I am the author. This is not a witness statement, and that should be made clear to the witness and not posed to him as if there are two statements out there. What we have is a proofing note and the unsigned information report that General Tolimir has already questioned the witness about, again which is not a signed statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, take that in mind and please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I had that in mind, and I said that I was quoting the document, and I called it a Prosecutor's report. I was just reading a quote to the witness, and I also quoted a portion of the witness statement in -- of the witness testimony in the Popovic case. I don't see that there is any problem there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, please don't be concerned about this. This has really nothing to do with you. Could you please tell us who organised this gathering when Morillon came to Srebrenica in March 1993? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I couldn't really answer your question, because I was not an employee of any of the state institutions, but I think -- my assessment is that this was probably a spontaneous gathering of the people, because they were hungry, cold, and I think this initiative just came spontaneously from -- by these people and these refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please, when General Morillon went to Srebrenica were there only Srebrenica people there or were there people from other towns around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No. There were a lot of people, displaced persons from the surrounding villages, towns, the municipalities of Zvornik, Vlasenica, Gorazde, people from those areas. So there were people from several different municipalities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this was also reported in the media, so let me ask you this: In this group of people who were outside the post office building, were there any representatives of the official government authorities or the party? Was there anyone there to meet General Morillon, or did they just let the citizens and villagers meet General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, when he arrived, I didn't really see him, and the talks were held behind closed doors. Now, who was with him, who met him, who saw him off, I really don't know. I didn't see it, and I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you've already answered the question, actually. It was organised, but you don't know who the organisers were. Have I understood your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. We were overlapping, and let me just repeat that your answer was, "Yes." I'm saying this for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you. Do you know by any chance that General Morillon testified before this Tribunal in the Milosevic case, transcript page 31975, on which occasion he explained that the events in Srebrenica in 1995 were a reflection of the events that had transpired there up until 1993, and he was referring to the activities undertaken by -- from the surrounding villages in the protected zone against the Serbian military? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the massacres committed by Muslim armed groups against Serbian civilians in 1992 and 1993? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a Muslim attack on the village of Kravica on the 7th of January, on which occasion about 60 people were killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. I know about Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that before the attack of the Serbian Army on Srebrenica there was an attack on Visnjica and the villages in front of the front line in the part -- in the area of Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, the questions you're putting are too difficult for me. I can't really answer them. I'm not a military person. I can only tell you about information and things I heard about. I heard about Visnjica and its fall a few days before Srebrenica. Now, how the whole thing evolved, whether it had been planned or not, I really don't know, so I can't give you any further information because I did not belong to the group of people, the insiders, who would know that. Maybe a military person, a soldier, or a military strategist could tell you more about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know whether there were any casualties among the BH Army in those operations that they conducted against these villages in Republika Srpska? Because you worked in a hospital, do you know whether there were any wounded soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, of course there were wounded people on a daily basis. They were brought to the hospital, and the number was growing. And because of the enormity of the work that we had, I had no time ask these wounded people how and where they had been wounded. My job was to help them in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us what you know. And now I would like to switch to the third group of questions that Mr. Thayer had already mentioned, and it relates to humanitarian convoys. He mentioned that he knew that you had already testified about humanitarian convoys and that you mentioned them in your statements. We're still in 1993. In your testimony in the Popovic case, you said that your mother and sister had left Srebrenica in -- on a UNHCR truck. This was in 1993. Is that correct? Would you like us to switch to private -- to a private session?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No, but that's how it was, exactly as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So your answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3934, lines 16 through 18 in the Popovic case, you said: "They left with convoys that had brought food. Since trucks were empty, people got on and they left for the free territory. Those are UNHCR trucks." Did I quote your words properly? Thank you. Does this reflect the truth? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You say they went to the free territory, which means that you did not deem Srebrenica to be free. Is that what you meant when you said free territory? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1993 -- what I saw in January 1993, the situation was unsafe, unstable, and it became more difficult by the day. So I and all the others felt that Srebrenica was a very risky area for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You provided a very broad answer to my question, but could you please explain. Did everybody believe the same? Did everybody share that opinion, the military and the civilian leaderships, that the area was not safe for families and that the only people who could stay there were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: To -- I according to what I think, able-bodied men were safer, and especially when their families were in a safer place, when their wives and children were in a place where their safety was guaranteed. Even if something happened, they thought that they would be able to save themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you're saying that it was common practice among everybody, among soldiers and the structures of authorities, as you said in the Popovic case, it was deemed to be safer for the families and children to live in the Bosnian federation? Is it true? I don't want to quote your words from the Popovic case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just by way of example, could you please tell us do you know that some of the leaders or army members sent their families away? You don't have to give us any names. Just tell us whether you know about such instances.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: You know what? Those who got on those trucks and left were lucky, I would say. It was not easy to reach those trucks. It was not easy to get on them, and it was not easy to arrive in their destinations. To be honest, I wasn't present when my mother and my sister got on one of the trucks, but I heard from the others that while the trucks were being loaded that a selection process was going on, that some got lucky without anybody -- anybody's assistance. They did not need to be supported by any leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your lengthy answer. Who was it who carried out that selection process that you had mentioned? Thank you. Was that UNPROFOR or was that another body that were authorised to do so in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I repeat, and I can only tell you what I heard, none of the UNHCR personnel was in charge. I suppose that it was the authorities of Srebrenica who were engaged in that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether soldiers left on those convoys as well, or was it just women or children?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Honestly, from what I heard, among the women and children and elderly there were also some able-bodied men. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us just approximately, you said that it was common practice when you spoke in the Popovic case whenever a convoy arrived, and we know how those lorries arrived, according to your estimate, how many people got on one truck? What would you say? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I really can't give you the exact figure. I only heard that there were some people who suffocated. So the lorries were overloaded. Many died before reaching Tuzla. This is the information that I have. I don't know. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you're talking about 1993 or some other year?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about 1993. I'm talking about humanitarian aid and -- humanitarian aid and the transport of refugees from there to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I thought that you were talking about 1993, because that's what you were recorded as saying in the Popovic transcript. We don't want to dwell upon that any longer. I'm happy with your answers so far. Tell me, am I right in saying that those convoys usually transported women and children, as was the case in your case, but there were also able bodied -- but that able-bodied men mostly stayed in Srebrenica unless they were really lucky to got on one of those lorries? Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me absolutely well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please tell us, while you personally did not leave Srebrenica with the rest of your family when you looked younger? As you yourself said, you were-- you were younger. Why didn't you take the opportunity and leave at that time?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Are we still talking about 1993?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, I didn't even try. And even if I had tried, I would not be able to get on any of those trucks. I would be automatically eliminated from there. I was not even present when those people were leaving. I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So I understand that you didn't stand a chance, that you didn't have anybody among the selection committee to put you on the truck. Thank you. Thank you, Witness. And now I would like to move on to another group of questions. I believe that we have exhausted the topic of convoys, departures, and we have dealt with the ambiguities in the Popovic transcript. If you don't mind, maybe -- maybe you think we should go into private session, because I would like to hear the year of your birth.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move into private session for the witness to tell us the year of his birth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment please. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Quite all right, Mr. President. I think out of an abundance of caution that should have been in private session. So I would ask, unless the witness feels comfortable with that information being in the public domain, that we go in closed session for anymore of these details which might possibly identify him, and I think we'll need a redaction if he obviously does have concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, is that the case, that you have concerns with the last answer you gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like all of that to be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. That will be done. Mr. Tolimir, will you go on with these kind of questions? You may -- you may decide that during the break. We will have our first break now. The court officer will assist you during the break. And we will redact the portion between line 6 and 11 of page 31. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, let's not repeat the year of your birth and so on and so forth. Could you please answer the following question. I'm going to sum up all those questions without going into private questions. Since you were at an age which, pursuant to Alija Izetbegovic's order, included you among the able-bodied men, were you subject to mobilisation? Were you a conscript? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I was not subject to mobilisation. I was not a conscript. I was a health-care worker who helped the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please tell us, health-care workers, were they listed as conscripts or those under work obligation, and did you as such enjoy some benefits, some monies in respect of that, anything? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Some health-care workers were conscripts, as it were, and as far as financial benefits are concerned, there were none. While I worked, I received a somewhat bigger quantity of humanitarian aid. I received more staple foods than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did everybody receive payment in kind, everybody working in that hospital, or were they paid in money by municipality or by some other body?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: At that time, we did not have our own currency in Srebrenica. I don't know if anybody received any financial assistance expressed in German marks or some other European currency. I don't know. I don't know. I didn't receive anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. And what about those who worked in the hospital before the war? Did any of them stay in the hospital during the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Since I was never in Srebrenica before the war - the first time I arrived in Srebrenica was in January 1993 - I don't know who worked in the hospital before the war. I can only assume that there were such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I'm asking you. There are people who say that they -- they worked there before the war. Some were almost nearing retirement. Did any of them receive any financial benefits or salaries?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer your question. I'm not sure. I can't give you a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wanted to avoid -- avoid closing the session and quoting the transcript. I'm going to show a document which does not indicate your name. This is 1D75. This is a payroll, a list of all the employees, and that list does not contain your name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it would be better to redact the question and place this -- this entire questioning in closed session. I think we were nearing the line in some of the prior questions with respect to potentially identifying the witness, but I think reference to this document in any form crosses that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the following questions we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see a reason to go into private session. I didn't say anything --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are in open session. I will have no further questions about that subject. I would like to ask you this, Witness: In the Popovic case you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Judge Nyambe has a question to the last issue, and then you can continue with another point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have a question for you, Mr. Witness. You have just said, correct me if I'm wrong, that when you worked in the hospital you are paid in kind. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. During that period while I worked there, as far as I remember, I received two pairs of boots. And as far as food is concerned, I received a few kilos of flour and some other staple foods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Another -- a follow-up question. Was this the normal practice? Was everybody else paid in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Everybody else was paid in the same way. I don't know whether there were any exceptions to that. I don't know whether anybody received more than I did. I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, the Prosecutor said that in your testimony you spoke about the shelling of the playground in Srebrenica when 60 people were killed, and he also included that in the summary. This was on page 3934, lines 2 and 3 of the Popovic case transcript, and I am going to put a few questions to you about that incident. You said on that occasion while testifying in the Popovic case -- can you see it? The page number is 3936, 3936, lines 7 and 8, and I quote: "According to some unofficial information, some 60 people got killed, and some 60 were either slightly or seriously wounded." However, on page 4045 of the same transcript, lines 5 and 6, you say: "This is information that I heard from the -- at the hospital when those people were admitted to be looked after in the hospital." Thank you. My question is this: If you worked at the hospital from 1994 and that incident took place in 1993, allegedly during the celebration of the day of Srebrenica, how come you could hear in the hospital how many dead and wounded there were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Some five or ten minutes before that I was in the clearing near the school playground, and there were a lot of young people there. Among them there were also my acquaintances. A few shells fell, and the information leaked that a tragedy had struck. That's when I returned to the scene to see whether I could recognise some of my acquaintances among those people, and I also wanted to check what had really happened. At first in the playground you couldn't really tell how many people were dead and wounded. However, a few hours later I went to the hospital, and I received information. I inquired, and I was told how many killed and how many wounded. I was told that about 60 people had been killed and that over 60 people had been either slightly or seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that information from an official source or did you just hear it from somebody working in the hospital? You yourself did not work in the hospital at the time, as you have told us yourself.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I heard that from a group of people who were at the very entrance to the hospital, and I believe that one of their own had been wounded, and that's how I learned about the figures. They were the ones who gave me that information. I did not receive the information from an official surgeon or somebody of that kind. Any officials were really very, very busy at the time. The hospital was understaffed anyway, so there was no time for any of them to talk to laypersons hanging around the hospital before they had been able to treat the wounded adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 3944 of the Popovic transcript case, you spoke about the period after the departure of General Morillon from Srebrenica, and you said that you had witnessed the consequences of the shelling in Srebrenica which had taken place during the celebration of the proclamation of Srebrenica as a protected area. And then on page 3936, you say, and I quote: "Let me put it this way: Serbs in the observation points were obviously supposed to notice the group of people who were gathered there. I don't know what happened. Some five or ten minutes later I passed the area, and I could see the dismembered human bodies, heads, and legs hanging -- thrown around. According to some unofficial information, some 60 people were killed and over 60 were either slightly or more seriously wounded."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Tolimir. The interpreters don't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I have to repeat anything? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. I think the witness understood your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was just reading something, a quotation, and now comes my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Where was this observation post or position that you're talking about here, and could Serbs actually -- were they able to observe the position of the place where these people had been killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, you see I assume that people actually assumed where the shells could have come from, and I think that it came from Bratunac or some -- I don't know exactly what that elevation is called. And of course they did reach Srebrenica, which means that Serbian soldiers were able to observe from an elevation the mass of people who were there gathered, and in this way they actually fired I don't know how many of these shells which unfortunately killed the number of people that I mentioned there, of young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you have occasion to travel the Bratunac-Srebrenica road? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I did not take the Bratunac-Srebrenica road, but I did to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you hear from someone that the lower-lying areas, for instance the Yellow Bridge, was there, whereas the Srebrenica hills were on a higher, slightly elevated ground? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, I did hear of the Yellow Bridge, Zuti Most. It is true that it is in the foothills of those hills around there, but around Srebrenica there are a lot of hills. And I also have to point out that the Republika Srpska Army was deployed on these favourable, as it were, elevations from where they could control and reconnoiter and observe the situation in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, this is your own assessment and the assessment of the civilians, citizens there, that the army could have seen or observed from somewhere that group; correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in the Popovic case you talked about the observation post of the Republika Srpska Army at length, but now we see that it was actually something that you just assumed and concluded. But now -- and when you asked whether -- when you were asked whether there was in Srebrenica the 28th Brigade -- Division of the BH Army, you said, I quote: "That was a question that you should have put to someone from the army." So on page 4043 you say, from lines 21 through 25 you say in answer to the question -- to the following question: "Do you know that the 28th Division of the BH Army was in Srebrenica?" To which you reply, I quote: "That is the question that you have to put to an army officer. I am just a health worker, and I really cannot answer that question." My question for you is this: If you're not competent to answer questions that relate to the military, can we then conclude that this is just your lay-conclusion as to where the positions could have been or something that you heard from another person or third persons, because in order to determine whether something was an observation post or not, you need to have military experience, and you couldn't even answer the question about the 28th Division. So could it be that you did not perhaps understand the question that was put to you then or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, there were some troops in Srebrenica, but what those units were called I really don't know. Some people had some camouflage uniforms on, but you couldn't really read. It didn't say who they were and what their unit's name was, so I don't know what the name of the unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever have occasion to be in the hospital when some wounded were brought in from the front line? Did you have occasion, perhaps, to fill out a form about those wounded and such information as to what their names were, what units they came from and so on?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I never filled out any forms myself, but there were cases where, of course, military personnel was also admitted to the hospital, and of course they were provided medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, please, were the people who had been killed, were they buried publicly, and did you attend the -- their burial? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I never attended any burial myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, were the people who had been killed both able-bodied men and civilians? Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to make clear for the record what exactly we're talking about here. Are we still talking about the shelling of the playground in April of 1993, or are we talking generally about admissions to the hospital at some other time. I fear the record is a little unclear on that -- on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tolimir, could you please clarify this for the proper answer you want to get.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the witness understood me. We are talking about the individuals, the people who were killed on the field or in the playground, and I was asking the witness whether among those killed there were civilians and military personnel, and I haven't received an answer yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. The place where these people were killed, at that place most people who were killed were civilians, but there were among them people also wearing camouflage uniforms, which probably points to them being conscripts or able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I can assist you here. Was this an organised gathering? Was there some occasion for this gathering, and who were the participants and who organised it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I don't know who organised that gathering, but I know that young people attended this gathering. They gathered there, the youth, because there was a cease-fire, and it was a kind of celebration. There was a bit of dancing, some music playing, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not going to quote the Popovic transcript again, but you said this was a celebration on the occasion of Srebrenica having been declared a safe area. Did I understand you correctly, and is that how it was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me well. Most probably the cause for this celebration was the declaration of Srebrenica as a safe zone, and because of all the suffering that people had been through before that. They wanted to celebrate this event, and they probably wanted to start their life -- restart their life again and try and live a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you well, then that would mean that that gathering must have been organised by the civilian or military authorities, because people don't just go out and celebrate anything. So this was a celebration on the occasion of the declaration of Srebrenica as a safe zone. Did the army also participate in this celebration? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, in my assessment, and I believe that most of these people were young people, there was a school there and young people were in the school, and they were probably the ones who organised this celebration. They got some music playing. And for that kind of gathering you really didn't need any approval by any authorities, and I assume and I suspect that at that time the authorities weren't really functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure I understood you clearly. Could you please tell me whether the army also participated in this celebration? I apologise for repeating my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: As far as I could see, most of those present were young people. There were boys 13 years old who had camouflage T-shirts on. I can't really say or confirm that they were military personnel. They may have just worn those T-shirts as kind of propaganda, but there were some soldiers there, too, but at that time a lot of people actually found pieces of clothing, military clothing, and sometimes would wear them. So I can't really say for sure whether there were military personnel or not, but most of the people there were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was a celebration organised by the authorities, and some people had uniforms on, but whether the army participated, whether the authorities participated when the celebration or if it was a spontaneous gathering, can you tell us anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think your quotation was not correct. You said, "So this was a celebration organised by the authorities." The witness has told you that he doesn't know anything about the involvement of official authorities. And the other parts of your last question are already answered, I suppose. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor said here, and also in the Popovic case, they talked about the celebration of this day when Srebrenica was proclaimed a safe zone, and I just wanted to know who organised this, whether it was the authorities, the civilian authorities, the military. I never actually got an answer. I don't know if you understood the witness, but I did not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the end of the day this is a question we have to give some weight to this examination, of course, but I think you repeatedly put this question to the witness, and you got the answer he can provide you with. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was just looking for a yes or no answer, but I accept your suggestion, and I will ask the witness this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you actually differentiate between a military person, a civilian, a conscript, a person on work obligation? So was this something that you could actually tell in Srebrenica? How did you actually -- how could you tell who was a civilian, who was a military person, who was a police officer, who on work obligation in Srebrenica? Can you tell us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: As for Srebrenica, and whether I was able to conclude who was a military person and who was a civilian, I have to say that it was difficult to give an answer to that question, but as for me, when a person wore a uniform, I considered that person to be a military person, a soldier. However, there were minors who had pieces of camouflage uniform on them. So military personnel had full camouflage uniforms, but it was really difficult to tell there at that time who was a soldier and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not dwell any further on this question, but could you please tell us, in the Popovic transcript, on page 3540, in answer to the Prosecutor's question you said that there were people wounded by sniper bullets. My question for you is: Did you have occasion to see such wounded people or people wounded in that way, and did you have occasion to treat them? And how could you tell whether they were wounded by a sniper bullet, because a sniper would have to be nearby in order for the bullet to actually hit the victim. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Until 1995, there wasn't much sniper fire, but in early 1995, as the security situation deteriorated in Srebrenica and in view of the large number of refugees and lack of heating materials or firewood, people were forced to actually go into the hills and forests around Srebrenica and cut some firewood to prepare for the winter. And as time went by, people actually ventured further and further out in search for firewood. Some of them also went far afield looking also for some food, blueberries and so on, so that some of them, as I heard, were wounded by snipers. Some were killed. As far as I heard, there were some individual instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I understood you better. So people actually went close to the snipers. It's not the other way round. The snipers did not -- the sniper or the marksman did not come towards the people. They actually went out and got close to them, and that's how they were hit; correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, yes. People actually reached pretty close. They got pretty close to the front line, and that's how they got wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any army members who took part in sabotage activities from the safe area who were then wounded in those operations and you had occasion to give them medical assistance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there any wounded treated at the hospital who had been hit in combat operations on the front line or in operations that they were engaged in against the Serb territory and who became victims of sniper fire, and did you actually determine the type of wounds that these people had so that you could provide proper treatment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: These individuals who came close to the front lines, most of them, as far as I could observe in the hospital, were civilians. There was a soldier here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic transcript, on page 3941, lines 20 through 23, you say, I quote: "There were also wounded people in ambushes, and many of them in the end thought that Srebrenica was unstable and they tried to get to the free territory, and then they would run into ambushes. " You were testifying here about the period before July 1995. Could you tell us now, please, how frequent these attempts to leave Srebrenica were by those individuals that you described there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, I just said a moment ago that in early 1995, the humanitarian and security situation in Srebrenica deteriorated so that it was reminiscent of 1992 and 1993 when there was hunger and people even died of starvation so that they were forced to find food somewhere. In order to obtain some food, many people ventured out towards Zepa, and as far as I was informed, the Zepa authorities had reported to the UNHCR a larger number of refugees than there actually were so that they received larger quantities of humanitarian aid, and they had some food stocks. But as far as I learned, these people then had to cover a territory that was under the control of the Republika Srpska Army, scavenging for food or looking for food so that many of these people actually ran into ambushes or minefields in search of food. Another group of people or category of people, in view of the deteriorating humanitarian and security situation, tried to leave the enclave on their own initiative. They would find a group of like-minded people, and some of them then were wounded on the front lines. Whether in ambushes or in minefields, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I could understand from your answers, can I conclude that you are actually here referring to woundings in combat operations, ambushes, illegal crossings of territories and so on? Did I understand you correctly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. On page 3943, you spoke about some wounded officers. That was in the Popovic case. Those men were brought to the hospital where you worked. Had they been wounded in fighting on the line or in a different situation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry to be somewhat late to my feet. I just was able to read the prior question. We haven't been objecting to compound questions to this point. We've let, I think, most of them slide. I think this particular compound question may merit just breaking it down, because there are a series of questions over a number of topics about wounded people being treated, and then there was a summary compound question with a single yes, and I think that would be important to break that down. General Tolimir asked the witness about woundings in combat operations, ambushings, illegal crossings of territories and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I'm very sorry. Could you leave it for your re-examination perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Witness, did you recall the question of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, I don't intend to go back to the same questions or to break them up. I asked you at the beginning about the sniping incidents when they were killed, and your answer that they were -- that they were -- that they were killed on the front line, in the ambushes and so on and so forth, and then I quoted document 3D43, when the Prosecutor asked you about those officers. I always refer to the transcripts from your previous testimony. I'm talking about transcript page number 3D43 when the Prosecutor asked you whether those wounded were civilians, soldiers, officers, or somebody else. If you would care to answer, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir please be asked to speak slower, because half of his questions will not be interpreted and recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, did you receive the comment of the interpreters? You should slow down with your questions. Otherwise, some of the parts of your questions will not be translated and recorded. Thank you. Witness, the question, in fact, was: "Those men were brought to the hospital where you worked. Had they been wounded in fighting the line, or in a different situation?" That was the question. Could you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we talking about July 1995 or a period preceding July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: July 1995 is the period, and the page number is 3943, transcript from the Popovic case. That's what the Prosecutor asked. The Prosecutor asked you whether those were civilians or soldiers or both were brought to the hospital, and you answered both, and my question is how did you make a distinction between civilians and soldiers, because your answer was, "Both." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Both. That's the answer. Soldiers arrived who had tried to stop the attack launched by the Army of Republika Srpska, and in addition to the shells that fell all over the city, there were a lot of civilians who were wounded by the shells who fell in the upper and central part of the town, and the military, the troops, arrived from the lines where they had been trying to stop the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the same transcript, on page 3943, line 8, you speak about officers who had been wounded and brought to the hospital. Could you please tell us which officers were wounded and brought to the hospital? Can you remember their names? If not, just tell us whether they were killed in combat or whether they were killed in other situations and under different circumstances. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Those soldiers were obviously wounded in defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So you're saying that they were wounded in combat. And now we will move on to another group of questions. I believe that the Trial Chamber now understands that there could have been no sniping from the Serbian positions, that in order to launch sniper fire they had to move closer to Srebrenica. So there were no snipers close to Srebrenica. Srebrenica was in the depth of the territory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please put questions to the witness. You are not the witness. You made a statement now. Please put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness when he spoke about sniping incidents and people being wounded from snipers. I quoted that, and I said if they were wounded by snipers, where were they wounded, on the front line, in Srebrenica? Whether the sniping fire could reach Srebrenica from the front line. And that was the period that we had already discussed and to which Mr. Thayer reacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't agree with you, perhaps, when you say that snipers could not open fire on Srebrenica. When you look how far it is as the crow flies, I believe that they could. I even know that some of the Serb troops came as far as the town of Srebrenica. They could reconnoiter the situation that prevailed at such moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to say that those lines were further away from Srebrenica, or perhaps they were not, and I was asking whether the -- from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska you could actually reach or target Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir please be asked to speak slower, otherwise he will not be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, please slow down, Mr. Tolimir, if we want to have a good and convenient hearing. And again, this was not a question but your statement. You are not the witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, on page 3943 of the Popovic transcript, you spoke about wounded military officers who were brought to the hospital. Could you please tell us anything about that situation? When was that, and who were those individuals, and what were the circumstances of their wounding? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Three or four days before the fall of Srebrenica a large number of soldiers arrived from the defence lines. They arrived in the hospital. Some of them were slightly and others seriously wounded. Whether they were officers, whether they had any ranks, I don't know. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You also spoke about the circumstances of your leaving the hospital. You said that you left in a white coat and a first aid kit. That's on page 3943 of the transcript. So there you speak about the circumstances of your departure from the hospital. You left of your own accord. Can you tell us something about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: At the moment when I decided to leave the hospital, the state of chaos reigned among the health-care workers, as well as among the wounded who were hospitalised in large numbers. The hospital did not have enough capacity. People were lying all over the place, in the corridors, in the rooms, in the cellars. We had not received any orders from the authorities of the hospital. We didn't know what to do. So the health-care workers were forced to make their own executive decisions as if -- as it were. I stayed there until the moment I felt I was safe. However, at the moment when I realised that the moment was no longer safe, that the situation was no longer safe, when I heard shells and bullets falling on the hospital roof, then I decided to use my white coat that was bloodstained. I actually decided to take it off and leave it behind, and I just took a first aid kit, and that's how I left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic transcript you said that you did take the coat, the first aid kit, and that without any documents you left the hospital, and you said that you were following all the other staff who worked there. That's on page 3943 in the Popovic case. Could you please answer the following question: Did everybody from the hospital left the hospital and left together with you where you went, or maybe you followed them, or did you follow anybody's orders? Did you have anybody's guidance? Did you follow some insider information or any such thing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Most us were moving in the direction of Kazin Kutlici and further on, up to the front line, but fewer of us or fewer of them, rather, went in the direction of Potocari.
