utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you're saying that some went to Potocari and the others joined those who were trying to reach Tuzla on foot. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of you have any markings or insignia showing that you were affiliated with the hospital, the region, any unit? Any of us who had coats, did those coats show any markings of affiliation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I have to go back a little. You're mentioning white coats. As I've already stated and I repeated today, I had taken my coat off. God forbid for me to keep the coat on. There was no need for us to wear white coats. All the health-care workers that I could observe wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will not go back to page 3943. I leave it to the Prosecutor and the Court to look at that. I'm just asking you whether you in the hospital had any markings on the coats. Did you have your name tags or any IDs that would show to any interested parties that you were health-care workers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: You mean while we worked at the hospital? Most of us had nothing. I believe that only general practitioners had name tags on their coats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have IDs or maybe Red Cross markings or any such thing?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an ID while you were in Srebrenica at all?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So if the MPs stopped you, how would they know that you were a hospital employee without any documents? How come that you were not afraid that they would take you to the front line, because the mobilisation was on. How come you were not afraid?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: There were no controls. There were no curfews. Nobody ever stopped me during my stay in Srebrenica. Nobody controlled me. The hospital had my details and information. Everybody knew I worked there. Nobody ever controlled me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you graduated from the nursing school and the rest were doctors, did you know that Red Cross markings or markings of affiliation to a health-care institution should be worn if you wanted to have and enjoy privileges in the territory or when you were called for emergencies or when you wanted to prove your status in case you were imprisoned? According to Geneva Conventions, you would have been entitled to some privileges if you had sported such insignia or markings. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: The MSF or the Red Cross was there, and I was in an MSF car. I travelled to Suceska, to a school where we were supposed to inoculate children. I didn't have any IDs. The only thing that we had was markings on that car, the Red Cross markings which enabled us to travel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In transcript on page 3945 you spoke about -- on line 6 [as interpreted] and 21 and I quote: "The exit from Srebrenica in the vicinity of Kazan there was a valley, and in that valley there were ham operators who had managed to send the last report and ask for assistance because Srebrenica had already fallen in the Serb hands. However, they received information to wait and that NATO Air Force would act and that people should not leave Srebrenica yet." Do you remember that you stated that on page 3945, lines 16 through 21 in the Popovic case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who these ham radio operators were and whether they belonged to some radio -- amateur ham radio operators association, or whether they belonged to some military unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: They belonged to the amateur ham radio operators, and this enabled them in view of the blockade of Srebrenica to maintain contact with their loved ones who were in some other country or whatever. I don't think they had any influence or any impact on the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell me, then, where they got the information from about NATO air-strikes and that they shouldn't leave Srebrenica yet? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, I actually caught up with a large group of people there, and that's where I also met the hospital director. This was in Kutlici, and that's where all these amateur ham operators were, and they told us that we should wait a little longer, that the upper parts of the town were already under Serb control. They had sent out that report, but as they said, we should wait a little longer, that there would be NATO air-strikes, and that this was on the final reckoning. However, indeed a few minutes later we heard NATO aircraft overhead. Some of them did drop a few bombs, at least that's what I heard, but then after a while they disappeared, which to us was a signal that we should wait no longer and that we should set off on our journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether these amateur radio operators, as you said, provided information to the NATO Air Force, and how did they actually prevent this from getting actually intercepted by the Republika Srpska Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Of course they had no contact with NATO, with the NATO Air Force. They didn't send such information to them. I assume that they were in touch with the state institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, maybe in Sarajevo, and maybe -- and I think that they, the authorities, actually sent them all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3945 of the Popovic transcript, in your testimony at line 25 you said that: "On the outskirts of Srebrenica," I quote, "I saw a large group of prominent people." And on page 3947, you said that there were, I quote: "People such as the hospital director, radio operators, people from the municipal authorities who were actually planning on the route to take and whether they should wait for NATO aircraft or just try to reach the free territory."

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Of course I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, as you see, then, the group that you were in also included all these people who would decide on who would leave, those people who decided on who would be actually selected to leave Srebrenica or not, and that these people were actually in the group with you and they were waiting for the outcome of NATO air-strikes; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, again if we can have some citation to the record, because I'm not familiar with it, where there was testimony about selecting who would be able to leave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us with the correct quotation, with the reference in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's page 3945, line 25, of the Popovic transcript. And the witness in his testimony then said the following that on the outskirts of Srebrenica, I quote: "I saw a large group of prominent men." And on page 3947, he said that there were there such people as, I quote: "The hospital director, ham radio operators, municipal authorities members who planned the route on which we were to proceed and whether we should wait for NATO air-strikes or continue on our way, uncertain way towards the free territory." And this witness confirmed that this is what he said during his Popovic testimony. If there is any other matter that needs to be cleared, I'm prepared to repeat my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, so I would ask that the question -- the questions reference any selection of people who would be permitted to leave Srebrenica be removed since that is not part of the record and it's a misstatement of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you repeated now -- you quoted now the transcript in the Popovic case correctly. What is now the question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who in this group decided on the route to take, whether they should go to Potocari or try to break through to the free territory, the Muslim federation territory towards Tuzla? Could you identify an individual or a group which by way in their official capacity actually stood or were behind that decision?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, in the general chaos that prevailed there, no one could really determine the route that we should all move on. However, there were prominent men from state institutions at the head of that group, and they decided that we were to take this route via Konjevic Polje-Cerska-Kamenica and on to the free territory. However, I repeat, we were all left to our own devices. We all tried to find a way to protect ourselves. Many people actually followed different paths or different routes. So it was really an individual decision that people made there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful. Now you just said that these were people who were from government authorities or municipal authorities and that they were waiting for NATO air-strikes, that you should wait for NATO air-strikes. Now, this could not have been said by just an average Joe. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: The order to wait for the NATO air-strikes came from the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not from the chief of the Srebrenica municipality. This came from the state, from the government authorities, and they were waiting to hear what was going to happen next, and then that channel of communication with the state authorities was disrupted so that there was no further communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood your answer. On page 3948, you mention a group that head towards Potocari, and you say that it was a mixed group, that there were civilians, able-bodied men, women, and elderly people in it. This is on page 3948 in the Popovic testimony. Now, my question for you is: Did you get an order to move towards Tuzla, or could you decide freely whether you were going to join this convoy or go towards Potocari? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: This was left to everyone to decide on for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the column that you were in, was there a special medical unit, or were you professional medical staff the only ones who provided medical assistance to people, or was there a military medical unit there who were part of those units there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, there were also nurses, male nurses there, who were members of those units and who also worked in the hospital, and there were members of those military medical units. However, we did not belong to that medical unit, Medical Corps unit. We were separate and independent. But in the event of a serious wound, someone being seriously wounded, they couldn't really do much. And in those cases, then there would be the involvement of general practitioners and professional medical staff and nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So units did have these medical units, and they were part of military units, whereas you were just hospital staff. Is that correct or not? And you were separate.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get, receive any instructions, requests, orders regarding medical assistance that you were going to provide? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: On this journey of death, as I call it, I personally did not receive any information or instructions. However, if somebody was wounded, I would be informed of that, and of course I would go and administer medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said here that you were at the forward end of this convoy; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: When we left Srebrenica, I was at the forward end of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You mention later on that you returned and went back to join the very end of the convoy; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No, I did not go to join the back end of the convoy, because it was not possible to actually get through to the back end of the convoy, which had actually been cut in half for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There is nothing at issue here, and it has nothing to do with you personally, but on transcript page 3955, you say the following, I quote: "The medical staff received orders to go back and take care of the wounded and the dead. However, after we went back for some 500 metres or so, we were unable to move forward to the dead and wounded because of the shelling." My question to you is: Who issued this order to the medical staff to return, and who issued this order to -- for you to move back towards the end of the convoy and take care of the wounded and the dead? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I don't know who issued that order, but these -- such orders came from almost anyone. We would say, "Well, come on. Let's go back to the end of the column." The column was cut off. There were a lot of dead and wounded. So we tried to go back and tried to break through and reach them, but because of the shelling we were unable to do so, and we went back to the place where we were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this end of the convoy actually run into an ambush or was it -- did something else happen there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, whether there was an ambush or whether this was called by the shelling, I don't know, because I never reached the spot where that happened, so I can't really answer your question. We just heard that there were many casualties, dead and wounded, but whether they had run into an ambush or whether they were shelled, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But can you tell us, did you learn how many casualties there were, how many dead and how many wounded? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: We never received the exact number. We were just told that there were a lot of casualties. There were many wounded and dead, but we didn't -- we weren't told the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you say "a lot," is that over a hundred, under a hundred, a hundred people? How are we to understand that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer specifically. I really can't give you a figure. I'm not sure what they went by "many." I really don't know whether they meant in the tens or in the hundreds. I really don't know. But this was a long convoy, some 7 to 8 kilometres long. I can just say that I wasn't there, and I don't really know the number of those people who were killed on that first occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear from anyone an approximate number of casualties in this incident? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I did not, because soon thereafter there was another major tragedy and so that I never heard about any figures about that first incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, about that second major tragedy that you mentioned? What did you hear about that, and what are you referring to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: We were in a valley among the hills. The names of the hills I don't know because I'm not familiar with the area. In any case, we were somewhere above Kravica, and that road or that corridor was not far from there. I heard bullhorns and Serbian soldiers calling up to the Muslim population who were hiding in the forest to surrender. Actually, it was an ultimatum, and according to that ultimatum if they didn't surrender until I don't know when, I can't remember, whoever was found in the forest would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you give us the date? Was that on the 12th or the 13th of July, 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: That was on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Popovic case, on page 3975, you spoke about that, and you said that the column that you were moving in came under artillery fire and that you had a lot of casualty in the column. There were a lot of wounded and dead. My question is this: Firstly, do you remember that; and secondly, did you provide assistance to any of the dead and wounded? How many did you register? Were there any dead and wounded falling in your vicinity so as to allow you to assist them?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: As soon as we started moving there were dead and wounded, but I don't know how many. These people were not tended to. We were waiting for nightfall in order to cross the corridor, in order to cross an asphalt road. At that moment I had a feeling that a huge tree trunk fell upon us, and from that moment there was chaos, wailing, screaming. People were falling. Some others were shouting, "Don't leave the wounded behind." It was dark, and it was very difficult to assess the number of wounded and dead in that opening. I stepped over the dead. The information reached us to go back, not to leave the dead and the wounded behind. We did not have any stretchers. There were some blankets, though, and with three other friends I grabbed a wounded by the legs in order to carry him. It was night. The terrain was not easily accessible. At that moment a burst of fire slayed my two friends. At that moment around me shrapnel was falling and the particles of earth. That's why I had to throw myself on the ground and roll myself down a valley up to a brook.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When was that? What date was that? What month? What date? The event that you just described, when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: On the 12th, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke, on page 3958 in the Popovic case, lines from 1 through 5, that on the 13th of July, and I quote: "We received information from the front of the column, I believe from the military leadership. I don't know exactly. In any case, we were told to go back because according to that information the last part of the column had been cut off and there were a lot of wounded and dead." Is this the second instance or was that the first instance when you were told to go back? Were there two such instances of you being told to return?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: That referred to the first part of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us the name of the place where that part of the column was where there were a lot of wounded and dead? Close to which place was that part of the column?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this may be a interpretation or some other issue, but the witness's answer doesn't seem to correspond with the question that was asked by General Tolimir. Just so we have can have a clear record, I would ask that the question and the answer -- the question be asked again, because the question had to do with were there two instances, two events, in other words, and the witness referred to a part of the column as opposed to answering the question, so I just want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll repeat the question. On page 3955 in the Popovic case you said, and I quote: "After a while, we received information that the last part of the column had been cut off and that the column came under heavy shelling and that there was a lot of wounded in that part of the column." And then you continued and I quote again: "The health-care personnel received an order to go back and tend to the dead and the wounded. However, when we returned some 500 metres, we could not reach the dead and the wounded as a result of heavy shelling." You said that that happened once the column started moving. Was that on the 13th, or was that on the 11th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this was actually a different question now. This was actually the third question, in fact. I think -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The situation is quite confusing for the witness at the moment because we have different instances, different occasions, and the questions are slightly different, and you quoted now another part of the Popovic transcript, not that one on page 3958. I think it is now a convenient time for the second break, and you should prepare your further questions so that you can hopefully close your cross-examination quite soon. What is your indication, Mr. Tolimir? How many time is needed for the finishing of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But here we're talking about two different places where the column was shelled and cut off in two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. This was not my question. Can you indicate how much time do you need for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that I have about 40 more questions according to my plan, and I'll try to finish all of them by the end of the day, but I would kindly ask the witness to provide shorter answers. All of the things that I'm referring to were said during the Popovic case, and I have to identify all of those things. I have to refer to every date, every event. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is your right. This is very clear, but the answers of the witness are very short and to the point. We have our second break now, and we will resume at 1.00, and then there are 45 minutes left, and hopefully we can finish for today, and it's not very -- I think it's not possible to start with the next witness after this indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With that said, may we release the witness who has been waiting for some time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We adjourn and will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, in order to cut the long story short and comply with the Presiding Judge's request, could you please tell us how many times did you stop as a result of ambushes and combat activities as the convoy moved from Srebrenica to Tuzla? How many times was that convoy cut off and stopped in its advance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: The first time the column was cut in half was on the 12th of July, and it no longer looked like a convoy. It -- the people dispersed and the convoy looked like groups of people. Many times the convoy was no longer a convoy. There were just groups of people, and different groups faced different ambushes, different problems, and so on and so forth. In other words, there were no two groups that proceeded in the same way and that had the same journey to the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So the first time it happened on the 12th, and that's when you suffered a certain amount of losses, but you don't know how many casualties you had on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did it happen on the 13th for the second time where you returned to the end of the column on the 13th? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: On the 12th in the evening there was a major exodus, and the people were then dispersed once and for all. It was my turn, there were a lot of wounded, and I assume that the Serb soldiers got mixed up with that group of people, and from that moment on there was no longer convoy to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how many groups did the column break up into, and how many people remained walking towards Tuzla after that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, in the evening, I was cut off from the column. I stayed behind, and the column continued advancing towards the free territory. How many people there were in the first column I can't tell you exactly. I can't give you a -- even a rough estimate. According to some unofficial information, there may have been a thousand or so people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you talking about the thousand who remained or the thousand who kept on moving forward?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I'm talking about those who kept on moving forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us -- are you saying that that was a smaller part of the total number of people who had set out from Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how many ambushes did you encounter in that part of the convoy where you were?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I've already told you. The first time the column was ambushed and cut in half, and from then on there was no convoy to speak of. There were just groups of people who gathered and tried in their own ways to find exits and to find their own directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And the part where you stayed until the moment you were captured, did that group encounter ambushes? Did it encounter combat activities on its route?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: As we were walking towards the place where I was arrested for over 11 days, I walked with some dozen groups. For example, you were in one group, and then shells start falling or you're ambushed, then the group disperses. Some people get killed. Some are left behind wounded. Some survive, and those who survive, they continue on their own tracing their way through the forests, across the brooks, and on that route encountering others with whom they then form groups of some 10 or 15, and again they encounter ambushes. The group disperses again and are reassembled again. That's how I changed some ten or so groups until the moment when I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether there were any losses in those groups? Did you see suffer more losses, and did the number of casualties surpass the number of those who reached a final destination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes. The number of casualties surpassed the number of those who reached the final destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What are you saying? Were there more people who were killed, captured, alive, ambushed, what?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: More people were killed in ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judging by the number of survivors, could you please give us an estimate how many people were killed in the convoy moving towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I'm sure that there is an exact figure. I can't give you that, but I would say that the total number was 7- to 8.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What 7- or 8.000, killed or what?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Killed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. How many survived if 7 to 8 were killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I don't know how many survived. I believe that there are statistics. I can't give you any answer. I don't know. Many people ended up in camps. Some were exchanged or not. I can't give you the exact number of those who started moving with the convoy. So it's impossible for me to say how many survived. And as far as I know, according to what I hear, there were 7- or 8.000 of those who were killed and who never made it to the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You're talking about the figure mentioned by the media. I'm just asking you about what you saw about the part of the convoy that you moved in, the ambushes, the combat activities that you witnessed yourself. How many people were killed there while the column was moving from Srebrenica to Tuzla? Just tell me what you saw.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: The situation was horrendous. There was no way for me to count all the killed and wounded. And when we had to cross asphalt roads, we did that during the night. So as we were crossing the road, I would be stepping over dead bodies, and there was no way for me to see how many there were, to count them. I was trying to survive, and I just kept on moving. I don't know how many people got killed. In any case, I encountered a lot of bodies on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you were trying to avoid the ambushes, the combat activities, could you give me an approximate number of the bodies that you saw, encountered, or mentioned? You say that there were a lot. How many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, he said that it was dark, he couldn't see the whole number of bodies, and therefore he is not able to gave an estimation. I think you should leave it with that. You got an answer already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but I'm not referring just to the night when it was dark. I'm referring to the entire period when the witness spent on the way in this convoy until he was captured. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give an estimation, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will give you an approximation, but how accurate that will be, I really don't know, but what I was able to determine in that state of mind that I was in, there were certainly a few hundred, maybe 2 or -- 200 or 300 bodies that I had occasion to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This was on the stretch of road between Srebrenica and Snagovo - am I correct? - while you were in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Up until the moment when I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us, please, how many armed men were there in the column around you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I said that there was no convoy or column any more. These were just scattered groups of people. You know, like a pack of wolves or a group of sheep. The column was broken up. There were groups being formed in the woods. Part of the column continue on the road, but others remained behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us, please, what date it was when you were captured? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Of course I can. I remember that date very well. That was on the 22nd of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How many men were you with when you were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: There were five people with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You say on page 3970 in the Popovic transcript that you spent two days and two nights in the rooms together with the soldiers who had captured you, and I quote, you said: "We slept on mattresses on which the soldiers also slept so that I was with -- among them." Did I quote what -- your words correctly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes. I was with them, but this was not a room. We were in open air, lying by a gravel road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm trying to find out is whether you were sleeping in the same conditions that they were sleeping in, because you said that you were sleeping side by side with them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Whether I had the same conditions that they had, I really can't confirm that. I only spent the first night there, and later on they put me -- they kept me separate and they tied me. I slept on the first night by the road, but of -- and then on the second night I slept side by side with them, but I was mistreated, and I was humiliated by them, so the conditions that I was in were not quite the same as theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But the conditions that was sleeping was -- the sleeping conditions and food, did you have the same food that they had?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: As for food, I have to be fair and say that indeed I did receive enough food while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in the Popovic case, you said that you were in Zlatna Voda near Zvornik. That's where you were captured, after which you were sent to Zvornik. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, I would like to correct you. I wasn't sent to Zvornik. What do you mean sent to Zvornik? How? I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I said you spent that time together with those soldiers in the so-called Zlatna Voda near Zvornik. Is that correct or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you sent to Zvornik after that -- or, rather, to Ugljevik?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes. Together with them I left on a bus to -- for Ugljevik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you went to Ugljevik. Were you taken there by the same soldiers who had captured you or by someone else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: The soldiers who captured me and with whom I spent those two days and nights there -- and the reason for staying there for those days was that the buses could not reach them, could not get to them. And as we were getting -- or driving through Zvornik and getting closer to Ugljevik, people got off the bus when they reached their destination so that by the time we reached Ugljevik, there were some four or five soldiers left of the group who had captured me, and then together we went to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you went together to the command in Ugljevik, and how much time did you spend there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Some 10 to 15 minutes, me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you asked for your personal details then as you said in the Popovic case? I quote: "In fact, they asked me for my personal details." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They asked for my personal details, my first and last name, the date of birth, place of birth, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they ask any other information of you in those 10 or 15 minutes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Not at that point in time, but that's probably because they received information from the soldiers who had captured me, because we arrived there in late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it normal to ask a prisoner of war for their information? I mean, was it better for you that you had been asked about these things or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Well, up until the moment when the police are -- the policemen who arrested me told me, when they said that they couldn't really tell me anything about what was going to happen to me next and what my future was going to be, that my life was still not safe, and for that reason we would have to go to the command where I would get an answer to that. So there was no talk about me being taken to a camp. That decision was to be made at the command where they would decide whether I would be killed or sent to the camp and so on and so forth. And after I provided my personal details I was sent back, and the group of policemen who had captured me came out a few moments later and told me that I would be taken to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were taken to the same place where other prisoners of war were taken; correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in Batkovic in -- late in the evening. I arrived at the hangar where there was only one bulb, light bulb, by the door, so I couldn't even see how many people there were inside or what it meant to be in a camp. However, in the morning I was able to see a number of people and recognise a number of people who were from Srebrenica, and I could also see that there were some people, wounded people, who had been treated at the Srebrenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But can you tell me, were these wounded actually people who had been treated at the Srebrenica hospital, or were they wounded immediately preceding your setting off on this journey? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: These were wounded people who had been wounded on the eve of the fall of Srebrenica and who remained in the hospital. Now, how they were transferred from the hospital to the camp, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that a number of wounded people from Potocari were transferred to the territory, towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I'm asking is that I'm surprised that they didn't join that group, because they must have been lightly wounded if they were in this convoy with you that had tried the breakthrough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was waiting for the answer, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the witness has made clear in his prior answers about where these wounded men from Srebrenica had come from, where he had seen them last, and now the general is incorporating a misstatement of the witness's testimony into his question. So I'd ask that the question be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this witness is capable to deal with this question as well. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The wounded people that I found in Batkovici camp were those wounded who had remained after I had left at the ward, hospital ward, who had been wounded preceding the fall of Srebrenica, and until I came to Batkovici camp I hadn't known anything about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, do you know were you still at the hospital when wounded people were sent from the hospital towards Potocari and then from Potocari on to Tuzla? Do you know anything about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I know that a large number of wounded were transferred to Potocari. However, where the other wounded ended up, I don't know. I don't know how they had been transferred to the free territory and whether they had. All I can confirm is that there were wounded in the camp and that they had remain in the hospital behind me and that they were later on exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So these wounded actually were in the column with you, moving onward. Am I correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: No, you're not correct, or maybe you misunderstood me. These were the wounded who had been wounded two or three days before the fall of Srebrenica and who had been admitted into hospital and then transferred to Potocari. What happened with them from that point on, I don't know. So how could they have gone on this journey? They were wounded. They were waiting for someone to save them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I was asking you about. So they were actually transferred from the hospital to Potocari and then to the Batkovici camp. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the wounded had been transferred to Potocari, and the group that I found was sent to the camp. However, that was just a small number of wounded people. What happened to the rest and what their fate was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who transferred these wounded from Potocari to the Batkovic camp? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question either very accurately, because these people were unwilling to provide any information. They were afraid that we were being actually -- that somebody was listening in on them, and they were afraid that they would divulge information. They weren't willing to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you know how they were transferred there? Were they transferred by the UNHCR or by the army, because this is a long trip. It's a four-hour drive, Srebrenica to Batkovici. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Of course they must have been transferred or transported by some vehicle. Who organised the transport, however, whether it was the Red Cross or the Army of Republika Srpska or a third organisation, I don't know. I did not ask them about this, so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you cannot answer my question. So they were wounded soldiers in Srebrenica, and now all of a sudden they were in Batkovici camp; correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your testimony in the Popovic case you spoke about the situation in Zepa, about the departure of some of the people from Srebrenica towards Zepa. Could you tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: I spoke about people who went to Zepa for humanitarian reasons. There was food there and other staples there. What is it that you want to know? What is your specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you this: Is it possible to embark on humanitarian travel from Srebrenica to Zepa during the war? Those were two separate territories both enjoying protection, but you had to cross the Serb territory. Were those departures legal/illegal, organised, not organised?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Those departures were not organised. People went on their own. Individuals crossed the territories. Why they did it. Try to understand. When you are hungry, when there is no food. I felt hunger on my own skin. I survived hunger, and I fully appreciate why people embarked on those journeys. There was no choice. They had to find food.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you spoke about them as wounded and as your patient. People who were wounded on such journeys, do you think that they were legitimate military targets? Was it somebody's intention to injure them or kill them on such humanitarian quests?

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Of course that nobody dared to embark on such a journey in groups. Those were individuals who lacked food. They didn't have much choice. They were between a rock and a hard place. It was either to find food or get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm asking you when they were crossing the terrain illegally, did they come across soldiers, minefields, ambushes, and were they injured as a result of such encounters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-022
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must -- we must have a look on the time. Mr. Thayer, how many minutes do you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you have three minutes left. You should try to finish. There are some procedural matters, for instance, with exhibits. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In that case, I would like to thank the witness for his answers and for being so specific in providing answers to my questions. And I would like to thank everybody who have assisted us. And I would like to apologise on my behalf and on behalf of the witness to the interpreters who have been exposed to some difficult times during the witness's testimony today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, thank you very much for your words, but you must understand the witness has to leave the Tribunal today and can't come back as the Chamber was informed, and therefore you had your full time. You have given the estimation of two and a half or three hours, and I think the witness was at your disposal. Thank you very much. In the presence of the witness I would like to ask you, you used three documents, one statement which was not signed, one proofing information, and the list of employees. Do you tender them as exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, not necessarily. I don't need to tender those documents into evidence because the witness is protected, but if it's all right, well, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you don't tender them, they will not be received. We learned that the Prosecution has listed several documents, I think five documents, which were not used in examination-in-chief. Perhaps you can -- you have asked with your motion to tender the transcript, and therefore perhaps we can do it in the following way: You send an e-mail to the registry, and of course to the Defence, with a list of these exhibits. Then they will be received with separate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we can proceed in that way also in future that would be very helpful, and we have it on the record to be identified. Sir, the Chamber would like to thank you that you came to The Hague again -- Mr. Thayer, I understood you correctly, you don't have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, the Chamber and all others present in the courtroom would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again to give your account, and we are grateful for this. Now you are free to return to your normal life and your normal activities. Thank you very much again, and the Court officer will help you and assist you leaving the courtroom when we rise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn now for the day and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
